Polyculture

Sow a mix, and let survival of the fittest decide what grows.

What is it?

Polyculture means mixing different seeds and sowing them together on one bed. You choose the mix, but after that nature takes over: which seeds germinate, how strongly each seedling grows, and what ends up dominating — that's no longer up to you.

You harvest gradually as things ripen: first the fast growers, then the slower ones. The strongest plants fill the freed-up space on their own.

Why does it work?

  • Easy to start: one sweep of the hand sows an entire bed.
  • Different crops make use of the soil at different depths.
  • Fast and slow growers complement each other over time.
  • The diversity reduces the risk of major pest outbreaks.
  • You quickly learn which combinations thrive best in your soil.

How do you apply it?

  • Mix seeds of crops with different growth speeds — for example lettuce, radish, carrot and spinach.
  • Temporarily remove the mulch from the bed, sow the mix and press it lightly into the soil.
  • Keep the soil moist until the seedlings are visible.
  • Harvest regularly whatever is big enough, without clearing the whole bed at once.
  • Let the strongest plants grow on and take over the space.

The biggest drawback

Polyculture and mulch don't mix well. A thick mulch layer makes it harder for small seeds to germinate, so you need to push the mulch aside temporarily to sow. As long as the seedlings are small, the mulch can't go back either — and that's exactly when the soil is most vulnerable to drying out and weeds.

So you temporarily lose all the benefits of mulching. That's a deliberate trade-off: polyculture offers variety and simplicity, but requires a period without soil protection.

Nuance

You only control the start. What happens after that is an interplay of soil, seed and weather — and that's exactly the charm of it.
